# Searching by File Type in ripgrep

When you search your files with ripgrep, you often want to focus on specific kinds of files. Rather than manually listing which files to look at or writing out the same glob patterns repeatedly, ripgrep's file-type system lets you search by category—C files, Python files, web files, and hundreds of others—all with simple flags.

## Understanding File Types

A file type in ripgrep is a label attached to one or more file name patterns. For example, the built-in `rust` type matches all files ending in `.rs`. The `c` type matches C source files (`.c`), C headers (`.h`), and a few variations. Instead of writing out these patterns yourself, you just reference the type by name.

ripgrep ships with dozens of built-in types covering common programming languages, markup formats, configuration files, and more. You can also create your own types when you need to group files that aren't covered by the defaults.

## Including Specific File Types with `--type`

To search only within files of a certain type, use the `--type` flag (or its short form `-t`). For example:

```bash
rg 'function name' --type rust
```

This searches for `function name` in all Rust files (files matching `*.rs`). The shorter form:

```bash
rg 'function name' -trusť
```

does the same thing. Both forms work; use whichever is easier to type.

You can specify multiple types in a single search. Each occurrence of `--type` adds another file type to search:

```bash
rg 'import' --type python --type javascript
```

This searches for `import` in both Python and JavaScript files.

## Excluding File Types with `--type-not`

Sometimes it's easier to say what you *don't* want to see. The `--type-not` flag (or its short form `-T`) excludes files of a certain type:

```bash
rg 'TODO' --type-not markdown
```

This finds all `TODO` comments everywhere except in Markdown files. The shorter form:

```bash
rg 'TODO' -Tmarkdown
```

is equivalent. Like `--type`, you can use multiple `--type-not` flags to exclude several file types at once:

```bash
rg 'console.log' --type-not test --type-not spec
```

## Viewing All Available Types

To see which file types ripgrep knows about, run:

```bash
rg --type-list
```

This prints every built-in type and the file patterns it matches. For example, you'll see entries like:

```
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
rust: *.rs
```

If you have many types and want to find a specific one, you can search the list:

```bash
rg --type-list | rg '^web'
```

This shows all types whose names start with "web".

## Creating Custom Types with `--type-add`

If ripgrep doesn't have a built-in type for what you need, create one with `--type-add`. The flag takes a specification in the form `typename:pattern`. For instance:

```bash
rg 'version' --type-add 'config:*.yaml' --type-add 'config:*.yml' --type-add 'config:*.toml' -tconfig
```

This creates a custom type called `config` that matches YAML and TOML files, then searches only within those files for the word `version`.

You can also use glob syntax with curly braces to be more concise:

```bash
rg 'title' --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb
```

This defines a `web` type for web files and searches through them.

A useful feature is including other types within a custom type. Instead of listing each pattern individually, you can combine existing types:

```bash
rg 'import' --type-add 'code:include:rust,python,javascript' -tcode
```

This creates a `code` type that automatically includes all the patterns from the `rust`, `python`, and `javascript` types. You can still add more patterns afterward:

```bash
rg 'import' --type-add 'code:include:rust,python' --type-add 'code:*.go' -tcode
```

## Important: Custom Types Are Temporary

Any custom type you define with `--type-add` applies only to that single ripgrep command. If you run the same search again without `--type-add`, the custom type disappears. This is by design.

If you want a custom type to be available every time you run ripgrep, add it to your configuration file. ripgrep reads settings from a `.ripgreprc` file in your home directory. Add lines like:

```
--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}
--type-add=config:*.{yaml,toml,ini}
```

to this file, and ripgrep will automatically use those custom types from now on. You can also use configuration files in your project directory—place a `.ripgreprc` in your project root, and ripgrep will find it.

## The Special `all` Type

Both `--type` and `--type-not` support a special value: `all`. 

`--type all` (or `-tall`) tells ripgrep to search in *whitelist mode*: it will only look at files that match one of ripgrep's known types. This is useful when you want to avoid searching miscellaneous files like temporary files or build artifacts that don't belong to any recognized type.

`--type-not all` (or `-Tall`) does the opposite—it searches in *blacklist mode*, looking only at files that ripgrep *doesn't* recognize. This can help you find loose scripts or unusual files that don't have standard extensions.

## Practical Examples

Here are some real-world uses:

**Search for function definitions in code, ignoring comments in documentation:**
```bash
rg 'def ' --type python --type-not markdown
```

**Find all FIXME comments in your source code (not tests):**
```bash
rg 'FIXME' --type-add 'src:include:rust,python,go' -tsrc
```

**Look for a variable name everywhere except in lock files and compiled outputs:**
```bash
rg 'my_variable' --type-not-add 'lock:*.lock,*-lock.json'
```

**Search only in configuration files:**
```bash
rg 'timeout' --type config --type ini --type toml
```

File types make ripgrep faster and your searches more focused. Rather than wading through results from unrelated files, you can zero in on exactly what you need.
